notes:
I could only do part of this job. My tool budget ran out after a single search, so these notes rest on three pages: **Enduring Word (David Guzik)**, **Matthew Henry on Blue Letter Bible**, and **Precept Austin's Exodus 31 page** (which quotes David Thompson, George Bush and Henry Morris). I couldn't open the Bible Hub or StudyLight commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit), NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or any denominational or Catholic/Orthodox sites. Because of that, parts 2 and 3 are mostly missing, as you asked me to leave out what I couldn't find. Verses without a note are verses none of the three pages discussed.

---

**v. 1–2**
- God picked the craftsmen himself, just as he picked Moses and Aaron. "Called by name" marks this as a specific personal choice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-31/
- Henry: God named the workers himself so there would be no fighting over who got the job and no envy of those chosen. Bezalel was to be the master workman. He came from Judah, a tribe God liked to honour. His grandfather Hur was "probably" the Hur who held up Moses' hands. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_031.cfm
- Henry passes on a Jewish tradition that Hur was Miriam's husband. If so, God's choosing Bezalel kept Moses from looking like he favoured his own family, especially since his brother Aaron had already been made priest. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_031.cfm
- Thompson: when God wants something built, he makes sure the right people are in place. Nothing in the project happened without Moses, who was responsible for the oversight as a whole. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**v. 3**
- Guzik: God gave Bezalel supernatural ability for the work. God counted this craftwork as just as spiritual, and just as dependent on the Spirit, as the work of Moses and Aaron. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-31/
- Thompson takes the four gifts one at a time, using Gesenius's Hebrew lexicon:
  - wisdom: God-given skill for making expert judgments in a field, which he says needs a right relationship with God
  - understanding: deep insight
  - knowledge: real knowing rather than guessing
  - craftsmanship: service God prescribes and enables

  https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary
- Henry: Israel had come out of slavery able to make bricks, not to work gold or cut gems. God had to supply that skill. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_031.cfm

**v. 5**
- Bush: the Hebrew word behind "carve" in "carving wood" means cutting grooves, whether in soil, metal, wood or stone. It is the same word as the earlier "cutting," which mainly refers to engraving names on the breastplate gems. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik: the gift was not for Bezalel alone. God put wisdom in all the skilled workers. But it was given "that they may make all that I have commanded," not for their own ends. He links this to Colossians 3:23. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-31/
- Henry: God hands out different gifts to different people for the good of the whole body. Moses was best suited to govern, but Bezalel was better suited than Moses to build. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_031.cfm

**v. 7–11**
- Guzik: the detailed list shows God wanted the work organised, with nothing forgotten. "According to all that I have commanded" points to a fixed pattern, a deliberate model of a heavenly reality. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-31/
- Thompson reads each item as a separate case of God giving the skill to build it: the tent, the ark, the mercy seat, the furniture. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**v. 12–13**
- Guzik: the Sabbath command comes deliberately at the end of the building instructions. Even the holy work of building the tabernacle was not allowed to override God's rest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-31/
- Bush paraphrases God as saying that important and urgent sacred work is still no excuse to cut into holy time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**v. 14–15**
- Precept Austin: repeating the death penalty shows how much this mattered to God. It points to Numbers, where a man gathering wood on the Sabbath was stoned. Because "put to death" and "cut off" sit side by side, it reads "cut off" as meaning death. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary
- Bush: "surely be put to death" is literally "dying shall be made to die." https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary
- Henry: despising the Sabbath is a crime for judges to punish. If people don't punish it, God will, unless the offender repents. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_031.cfm

**v. 16**
- Henry: the Sabbath was to be kept in every generation, one of the longest-lasting tokens of God's covenant with Israel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_031.cfm
- Bush: God and Israel were each to keep the Sabbath holy toward the other, which is why it is called a "perpetual covenant." https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**v. 13, 16–17: a real disagreement among these teachers.** Whether the Sabbath binds Christians is the one place where my sources clearly split.
- **Guzik:** under the New Covenant, Christians are not bound by the Sabbath (he cites Romans 14:5 and Colossians 2:16–17). The lasting principle is that our work for God must never overshadow our rest in Christ's finished work. He compares it to the moon eclipsing the sun, and says burnout comes when our work for God looms larger in our minds than his work for us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-31/
- **Thompson:** this passage settles the question. The command is addressed to "the sons of Israel," so the Sabbath belongs to Israel, not the Church. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary
- **Henry Morris:** for Israel the Sabbath was perpetual. But because it existed long before Israel was called, it is also a permanent reminder to all people that God's finished work of creation matters. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**v. 18**
- Guzik: these commandments really were "written in stone," not provisional. The first tablets were destroyed. Their replacements went into the ark, later joined by Aaron's rod and a jar of manna. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-31/
- Henry:
  - Writing the commandments down made them a lasting memorial.
  - Stone shows the law would last, and also shows how hard human hearts are. It would be easier to write on stone than to write anything good on a sinful heart.
  - He says some think angels prepared the tablets.
  - He contrasts law given through Moses with grace and truth through Christ.

  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_031.cfm
